title: If He took the ten
hookLine: what could the ungrateful say if the ten were taken too

lines: A QUESTION THAT TURNS THE HEAD.
cards: Back to the birthday table. The child is still sulking over the eleventh present. Now take the whole table away.
Not ten and a missing one: nothing. No cake, no wrapping paper, no party. What would there be to complain about then?
Who would there be to complain to? It's a question that stops a sulk in its tracks, and it isn't asked to frighten anyone. It's asked to turn the head around.
Guru Arjan asks it in the very next line, and then, surprisingly, he doesn't leave anyone at the empty table.

teach.h: IF HE TOOK THE TEN AS WELL.
teach.b: The line goes: ek bhee na dei, das bhee hir lei. If He gave not even the one, and took back the ten as well. Then: tau moorhaa kahu kahaa karei.
Then tell me, what could the fool do? Moorhaa is a blunt word: the foolish one, the one not thinking. The answer is in the silence after the question.
Nothing. No court to appeal to, no account to draw on. Everything on the table came from the same hands.
So the stanza goes on: jis thaakur sio naahee chaaraa.
With the Master before whom we have no leverage, no say. Taa kau keejai sad namaskaaraa: to Him, bow, always. That could sound like fear: bow, because you have no choice.
But the next line changes the whole stanza.

Jaa kai man laagaa prabh meethaa: in whose mind God has come to taste sweet. Sarab sookh taahoo man voothaa: every comfort comes to live in that mind. Meethaa is sweet, the taste of sugar on the tongue.

So the sum turns into something else. The person who sees the ten and thanks for them isn't cornered into bowing. They've started to love the Giver, and gratitude stops being a duty and becomes a taste.
From the empty table, to the full one, to the hands that set it.

how: Sikhs read this stanza in Sukhmani Sahib, and Sikh teaching treats gratitude to Waheguru as part of everyday remembrance rather than a separate ritual.

o: salty, like tears after a loss
sweet, like sugar on the tongue

games.q: if He took the ten — tap the pairs.
p: if not even one were given

s: the stanza ends on fear: bow, because you have no choice
it goes on: in the mind where God tastes sweet, every comfort comes to live.
the question is what the fool could do if the ten were taken too
the stanza says God comes to taste sweet in the grateful mind.

games.q: you've seen that everything on the table came from the same hands. in the stanza, what does gratitude become?
o: a taste: God comes to feel sweet.
a reason to ask for more.
games.why: jaa kai man laagaa prabh meethaa: in that mind God tastes sweet, and every comfort comes to live there.

practice: Pick one tiny thing, the warmth of a cup in your hand, a sock without a hole, light from one window, and notice it as if it had been taken away and handed back.
If you pray, thank the Giver for it in your own way; if not, just let yourself be glad of it, slowly, the way something sweet sits on your tongue.

wordCard.voice: Meethaa, sweet. Ek bhee na dei, das bhee hir lei: if not even one were given, and the ten taken too, what could anyone do?

orig.note: Gurmukhi: meethaa, sweet; in the stanza, the mind where God has come to taste sweet.

carryVoice: Your line: thank for the ten. The empty table asks; the full one answers. Day four hundred fifty-six, done.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
